description: The paper states that the explicitly estimated facial prior information (i.e., landmark heatmaps and parsing maps) and image features are concatenated and fed into the fine SR decoder. This is further validated by the paper's "upper-bound" model, which evaluates the network by replacing the estimated priors with ground-truth prior maps at the concatenation layer. However, the provided codebase concatenates the 128-channel intermediate feature (`p`) extracted from the prior estimation network with the image features (`f`). The actual prior maps (`prs`) produced by the final 1x1 convolutions are only used to compute an auxiliary loss and are entirely circumvented from the super resolution decoding process.
paper_quotes: Then, the coarse HR image is sent to the prior estimation network P and fine SR encoder F respectively,  p = P(y_c), f = F(y_c),  where f is the features extracted by F. After encoding, the SR decoder D is utilized to recover the SR image by concatenating the image feature f and prior information p,  y = D(f, p).

Inspired by the recent success of stacked heatmap regression in human pose estimation, we adopt the HourGlass (HG) structure to estimate facial landmark heatmaps and parsing maps in our prior estimation network... An 1 × 1 convolution layer follows to post-process the obtained features. Finally, the shared hourglass feature is connected to two separate 1 × 1 convolution layers to generate the landmark heatmaps and the parsing maps.

Fine SR Decoder The fine SR decoder jointly uses the features and priors to recover the final fine HR image. First, the prior feature p and image feature f are concatenated as the input of the decoder.

description: The paper states that the input sequence to the model is ordered as non-predicted tokens, followed by mask tokens, and then predicted tokens, denoted as `(x_{z<=c}, M_{z>c}, x_{z>c})`. In the official code, however, the `MaskedDataset` collator appends two sets of mask tokens to the end of the full permuted sequence `[x_{z<=c}, x_{z>c}]`, creating an intermediate sequence structured as `[x_{z<=c}, x_{z>c}, M_{z>c}, M_{z>c}]`. The model's forwarding logic subsequently splits the last set of mask tokens into the query stream and retains `[x_{z<=c}, x_{z>c}, M_{z>c}]` as the input for the content stream, differing from the order specified in the paper.
paper_quotes: Additionally, we add mask tokens M_{z>c} right before the predicted part, and obtain the new input tokens (x_{z<=c}, M_{z>c}, x_{z>c}) = (x_1, x_3, x_5, [M], [M], [M], x_4, x_6, x_2) and the corresponding position sequence (p_1, p_3, p_5, p_4, p_6, p_2, p_4, p_6, p_2), as shown in Figure 2a. In MPNet, (x_{z<=c}, M_{z>c}) are taken as the non-predicted part, and x_{z>c} = (x_4, x_6, x_2) are taken as the predicted part.
Figure 2: (a) The structure of MPNet. ... The predicted part x_{z>c} = (x_4, x_6, x_2) is predicted by the query stream.

description: The paper defines intersample attention as computing attention across samples in a batch: features of each sample are concatenated and attention is applied over the batch dimension, per head. Algorithm 1 explicitly reshapes to 1 × b × (n*d) so that the softmax attends over samples. In the code, intersample() reshapes q, k, v to 1 × b × h × (n*d) and calls the generic attention, which applies softmax on the last dimension after the key transpose; with that layout, the attention is taken across the head dimension (h), not across samples. Thus, the code effectively makes heads attend to each other within each sample, instead of making samples attend to each other per head as described in the paper. To follow the paper, q/k/v should be permuted and reshaped so that the sequence dimension passed to attention is b (e.g., 1 × h × b × (n*d)), with a corresponding transpose back after attention.
paper_quotes: We introduce intersample attention (a type of row attention) where the attention is computed across different data points (rows of a tabular data matrix) in a given batch rather than just the features of a single data point. Specifically, we concatenated the embeddings of each feature for a single data point, then compute attention over samples (rather than features).

Algorithm 1 PyTorch-style pseudo-code for intersample attention... def intersample_attention(x): # x is bznxd; b,n,d = x.shape; x = reshape(x, (1,b,n*d)) # reshape x to 1xbx(n*d); x = self_attention(x) # the output x is 1xbx(n*d); out = reshape(x,(b,n,d)) # out is bznxd; return out

In the code, the Linear, MergedLinear, and Conv LoRA modules initialize A with Kaiming uniform (a random initialization) and B with zeros, which mostly aligns with “B to zero” but not the exact Gaussian distribution. description: The paper does not document any special scaling or modification of the training loss beyond using standard classification loss, nor does it describe any difference between the loss used to generate gradients and the loss used during reconstruction attacks. In the code, the training (and victim-gradient generation) uses a Classification loss wrapper that returns 0.5 times torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss, thereby halving the gradient magnitudes. However, the reconstruction algorithm (GradientReconstructor) internally defines and uses torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss without the 0.5 factor to compute model gradients for its candidate images. Consequently, the attacker optimizes under a different loss scaling than the one used to generate the victim gradients, producing a systematic mismatch that is not reflected in the paper.

description: The paper describes a residual update between Koopa blocks where the next block’s input is the residual of only the time-variant component: X^(b+1) = X_var^(b) − X̂_var^(b). This follows from a block-level disentanglement X^(b) → (X_var^(b), X_inv^(b)), with Time-variant KP outputting both a fitted lookback X̂_var^(b) and a forecast Y_var^(b), and Time-invariant KP producing Y_inv^(b). In the code, each block disentangles residual into (time_var_input, time_inv_input), then computes a time-variant backcast and sets residual = residual − time_var_backcast, i.e., subtracting the backcast from the full residual (time_var + time_inv). As a result, the code’s new residual equals X_inv^(b) + (X_var^(b) − X̂_var^(b)), not just X_var^(b) − X̂_var^(b). Therefore, the code retains and propagates the time-invariant component into subsequent blocks, contrary to the paper’s stated residual definition.
paper_quotes:
Unlike KAEs [45, 44] that introduce a loss term for rigorous reconstruction of the lookback-window series, we feed the residual X^{(b+1)} as the input of next block for learning a corrective operator. And the model forecast Y is the sum of predicted components Y_{	ext{var}}^{(b)}, Y_{	ext{inv}}^{(b)} gathered from all Koopa Blocks:

X^{(b+1)}=X_{	ext{var}}^{(b)} - \hat{X}_{	ext{var}}^{(b)}, \quad Y=\sum\left(Y_{	ext{var}}^{(b)}+Y_{	ext{inv}}^{(b)}ight)

Our proposed Fourier Filter conducts disentanglement at the beginning of each block:

X_{	ext{var}}^{(b)}, \quad X_{	ext{inv}}^{(b)} = 	ext{FourierFilter}(X^{(b)}).
Time-variant KP simultaneously outputs the fitted input \hat{X}_{	ext{var}}^{(b)}, Y_{	ext{var}}^{(b)} = 	ext{TimeVarKP}(X_{	ext{var}}^{(b)}).

description: The paper describes a flow-matching training loss that predicts clean translations and rotations at time t and penalizes squared errors with a normalization factor of 1/(1 − t). Concretely, it uses terms of the form ||hat{x}_1 − x_1||^2/(1 − t) and ||log_{r_t}(hat{r}_1) − log_{r_t}(r_1)||^2/(1 − t). In the code, the implementation first divides the translation and rotation errors by (1 − t) (with clipping) and then squares them, i.e., it computes ((error)/(1 − t))^2. This makes the effective normalization 1/(1 − t)^2, not 1/(1 − t) as in the paper. The same pattern is used for both translations (r3_t) and rotations (so3_t).
